_note: The French pronunciation rules in the right-hand column of /pronunciation (AusspracheRegeln.astro), in teaching order. `match` is a regular expression tested on the lower-case word without an article: if it matches, the rule is listed under “For this word”. A rule without `match` is general and is never highlighted. `mark` (optional) is the strong (last) syllable of the word, shown in bold. Standard French of France is the standard (content-plan §1.1); where Québec French sounds different, the rule carries a `frCA` note. Rule ids: the old slot ids where the topic survived (r, s, h, ch, betonung, e-ende), the rest are new. Not yet reviewed by a teacher.

rules.title: Clean, short vowels
rules.text: French vowels are pure: the mouth stays in one position from start to end, so no glide. é is not “ay” (the English vowel in “day” glides), and o is not “oh-oo”. Unstressed vowels keep their full sound, so there is no weak “uh”. é is closed (été), è and ê are open (mère, fête): keep them apart, but don't worry if a French speaker from the north merges them.

examples.note: the same é at the end

frCA.note: In Québec, a short high vowel before a consonant is lax: petite sounds a bit like “pe-tsit” with a lax i. Long vowels glide: fête.

rules.title: Nasal vowels: an, on, in
rules.text: When a vowel is followed by n or m at the end of a word, or before another consonant, the n or m is not said. It only tells you to let the air go through your nose. There are three nasal vowels in the standard: an/en (vent), on (bon) and in/ain/ein (vin). un (brun) sounds like in for most speakers. Don't say the n at the end: bon is not “bonn” or “bong”. Before a vowel or a double nn/mm the n is said: bonne, une année.

examples.note: an/en: mouth wide open, air through the nose
on: lips round, no n at the end
ain is the same sound as in
nn: not nasal, the n is said

frCA.note: In Québec the nasal vowels are often longer and more open: vin is closer to [ɛ̃ː], and in a long syllable they glide a little.

rules.title: The French r
rules.text: The French r is made at the back of the mouth, not at the tip of the tongue: the back of your tongue comes close to the soft palate and air rubs through, a bit like a soft gargle. Practise from “ga” or from a gentle cough. It's neither the English r (tongue curled back) nor a trilled r (tongue-tip taps). Between vowels it can be quiet, at the end of a word after a vowel it is often very weak: bonjour, mer.

examples.note: r at the start, back of the tongue

rules.title: u and ou
rules.text: French has two sounds where English has one. ou is as in “you”: lips rounded, tongue back (tout, vous). u is a different sound: say “ee” (i) and, keeping your tongue where it is, round your lips as for “oo”. Lips matter: tu is not “too”, and rue is not roue. Swap them and you say another word.

frCA.note: In Québec, tu and ti are often affricated: tu sounds like “tsu”, dire like “dzire”. It is normal there; keep the France sound for exams in France.

rules.title: eu and œu
rules.text: eu is a third rounded vowel. Say é (as in été) and round your lips: that is the eu of deux, peu, feu (closed). Before a pronounced consonant, it is more open, like the vowel in “fur” without the r: peur, sœur, fleur. It is never ou: deux is not doux, peu is not pou.

examples.note: closed eu, at the end of a syllable

rules.title: The e muet (mute e)
rules.text: An e at the end of a word is not said: table sounds like “tabl”, but the consonant before it is. In the middle of a word and in short words (je, le, ne, de, que) the e is weak: it is dropped when the syllable before it is open, and said (like eu, short) when two consonants would come together. demain is often “d'main”, but je ne sais pas keeps its rhythm. In careful or sung speech, and in the south of France, an e muet is often said.

rules.title: é, è, ê, ë and the e before two consonants
rules.text: An accent shows the sound: é is closed (the mouth nearly closed, as in “say”, without the glide), è, ê and ë are open (as in “bed”). e before two consonants (elle, verre) is also open. The accent never moves the stress, and it can change the word: a / à, ou / où, sur / sûr.

rules.title: Liaison
rules.text: Liaison means a silent final consonant is said before a vowel sound. It is required between a determiner and its noun (les amis: lé-z-ami, un ami: u-n-ami), a pronoun and its verb (ils ont: il-z-ont), after one-syllable words like en, dans, très, and in set phrases (de plus en plus, petit à petit). It is forbidden after et (et ils), before an h aspiré (les héros), after a singular noun (un enfant intelligent) and after a name. In between there is optional liaison: only in formal speech. s and x are said as z, d as t: grand arbre, un grand_homme.

rules.title: Enchaînement: no breaks between words
rules.text: French joins words into groups, and a spoken consonant at the end of a word is moved over to the vowel that follows: il a sounds like “i-la”, une amie like “u-na-mi”. Don't put a small stop (a glottal stop) before a vowel as you may in German or English. The group, not the word, is the unit: je m'appelle is one flowing word.

rules.title: Silent letters
rules.text: Many letters at the end of a French word are not said: petit, grand, trop, temps, nez, beaucoup, and -er at the end of a verb (parler). The -ent of a verb in the plural is silent too: ils parlent sounds like il parle. The last letters c, r, f and l are often said (sac, mer, neuf, bol): think of the word CaReFuL. The feminine form brings the consonant back: petit / petite, grand / grande.

rules.title: Stress comes at the end of the group
rules.text: In French the words in a group have almost the same strength. Only the last syllable of the group is a little longer and higher. So, say “chocolat” as cho-co-LAT, and “un chocolat chaud” as un cho-co-lat CHAUD: stress moves to the end of the group. Don't stress the first syllable, as in English or German, and don't stress word by word, as in Spanish or Italian. Keep the rhythm even, like a row of beats.

rules.title: s, z, ss, c and ç
rules.text: s between two vowels is said z: maison, cuisine. ss is always s: poisson (fish) is not poison (poison). At the start of a word, s is s. c is /s/ before e and i (ceci, cinéma) and /k/ before a, o, u (café, cour). ç (cédille) is always /s/ before a, o, u: français, garçon. g is soft (like s in “measure”) before e and i: manger, girafe, and hard before a, o, u: gare.

rules.title: ch, j, g
rules.text: ch is sh as in “shop”: chat, chaud. j is the soft sound in “measure”, voiced and never like the j in “jam”: jour, jaune. g before e and i is the same sound: manger, rouge. Spanish and Portuguese speakers: j is neither a rasp (Spanish) nor “dj”.

examples.note: g before e is the same sound

rules.title: gn and ill
rules.text: gn is one sound, like ny in “canyon”: montagne, signe, Espagne. ill after a vowel is the sound y (in “yes”): travailler, fille, famille. At the start of a word and in a few words it is i + l: ville, mille, tranquille. Learn these three words and you know the main exceptions.

rules.title: h: muet and aspiré
rules.text: The letter h is never said. But there are two kinds. h muet acts as if it weren't there: l'homme, l'hôtel, les hommes (with liaison: lé-z-omme). h aspiré behaves like a consonant, but without a sound: le héros, les haricots (no liaison, no elision). A dictionary marks it. You must learn the common words: haricot, hasard, hibou, honte, hôpital is muet.

rules.title: qu, oi, ai, au, eau
rules.text: qu is /k/: the u is silent (qui, que, quatre). oi is “wa”: moi, voiture, trois. ai is è: j'ai, mais, maison. au and eau are o: chaud, beau, eau. ou is as in “you”, and in is nasal: always read the pair of letters as one sound.
